explanation: AWS RAM lets a resource owner share specific supported resources, such as VPC subnets, Transit Gateways, or license configurations, with other accounts or an organization without peering or duplicating the resource. Service control policies only restrict permissions, Transit Gateway connects networks but does not itself share subnets, and Control Tower sets up multi-account governance but does not perform resource sharing.

stem: An organization needs to deploy an identical CloudFormation stack containing a security baseline (a CloudTrail trail, a GuardDuty detector, and a mandatory IAM permissions boundary) to all 40 existing member accounts across 3 Regions, and automatically to any new accounts created in the future. Which approach is most appropriate?

choices.text: Create a CloudFormation StackSet with service-managed permissions and automatic deployment enabled for the AWS Organizations unit
Manually deploy the CloudFormation template in each account and Region using the console
Package the template as an AWS Service Catalog product and ask each account owner to launch it individually
Use AWS Config aggregators to push the template to each account

explanation: CloudFormation StackSets with service-managed permissions integrate with AWS Organizations to deploy and update stacks across many accounts and Regions from one operation, and automatic deployment extends that baseline to new accounts as they join. Manual per-account deployment does not scale, Service Catalog still requires each account to opt in rather than centrally enforcing deployment, and Config aggregators only aggregate compliance data rather than deploy stacks.

stem: A CloudOps engineer is deciding between using AWS RAM and CloudFormation StackSets to solve a multi-account requirement. Which statement correctly distinguishes the two?

choices.text: RAM shares a single existing resource instance across accounts so it can be used by all of them, while StackSets deploys and manages separate copies of resources created from a template in each target account
RAM and StackSets are interchangeable services that both replicate identical resources into every target account
StackSets can only target a single AWS account at a time, while RAM is the only service capable of multi-account deployment
RAM requires a CloudFormation template, while StackSets does not support templates at all

explanation: RAM is about sharing one existing resource, such as a subnet or Transit Gateway attachment, so multiple accounts can use that same resource, whereas StackSets provisions independent stack instances created from a common template into each target account and Region. They are not interchangeable, StackSets is explicitly designed for multi-account and multi-Region deployment, and RAM does not use CloudFormation templates at all.

stem: A company already manages infrastructure across AWS, Azure, and an on-premises VMware environment using a single infrastructure-as-code tool and wants to continue using that same tool for new AWS resources. Which third-party tool is commonly used for this multi-cloud infrastructure-as-code use case?

choices.text: Terraform
AWS CDK
AWS CloudFormation
AWS OpsWorks

explanation: Terraform is a widely used, cloud-agnostic third-party infrastructure-as-code tool with providers for AWS, Azure, VMware, and many other platforms, making it suitable for consistent multi-cloud provisioning. CDK and CloudFormation are AWS-native tools limited to AWS resources, and OpsWorks is a configuration management service, not a multi-cloud provisioning tool.

stem: A team is evaluating whether to migrate their AWS-only infrastructure code from Terraform to native AWS CloudFormation. Which is a valid tradeoff they should consider?

choices.text: CloudFormation is natively integrated with AWS services and typically supports new AWS features sooner, with no separate state file to manage, but it lacks Terraform's built-in multi-cloud provider support
Terraform state files are automatically managed and secured by AWS with no configuration required
CloudFormation requires a separate state backend such as Amazon S3 with DynamoDB locking to track resource state
Terraform cannot be integrated with version control systems such as Git

explanation: CloudFormation manages resource state internally as part of the service and often gets day-one support for new AWS resource types, but is AWS-only, whereas Terraform's state file must be explicitly managed and secured, commonly in S3 with DynamoDB locking, while supporting many providers beyond AWS. The other options invert these facts: Terraform state is not automatically managed by AWS, CloudFormation does not require an external state backend, and Terraform integrates well with Git-based workflows.

stem: A CloudOps team stores their CloudFormation templates and Terraform configuration files in a version control system so that changes are tracked, reviewed through pull requests, and can trigger an automated pipeline on merge. Which practice does this describe?

choices.text: GitOps-style infrastructure-as-code version control
Manual configuration management
Blue/green deployment
Canary release

explanation: Storing IaC templates in Git, reviewing changes via pull requests, and triggering pipelines on merge is the core practice of GitOps for infrastructure as code. Manual configuration management involves ad hoc changes without version control, while blue/green and canary are application deployment strategies, not version control practices.

stem: A CloudOps engineer needs to automatically remediate EC2 instances that AWS Config flags as noncompliant because Systems Manager Patch Manager reports missing critical patches. The remediation should automatically trigger a patch installation runbook whenever a new noncompliance finding appears. Which combination of services achieves this?

choices.text: Configure an AWS Config rule to detect noncompliance, and set an AWS Config remediation action that invokes a Systems Manager Automation runbook
Configure Amazon Inspector to launch a new EC2 instance whenever a patch is missing
Use Amazon CloudWatch Logs Insights to query log files for the word patch and email the results
Manually run Patch Manager scans and address findings when engineers have free time

explanation: AWS Config supports attaching automatic remediation actions, including Systems Manager Automation runbooks such as AWS-RunPatchBaseline, that execute as soon as a resource is evaluated as noncompliant. Inspector assesses vulnerabilities but does not launch instances as remediation, CloudWatch Logs Insights only queries logs, and manual scanning is not an automated remediation approach.

stem: What is the key difference between AWS Systems Manager Run Command and Systems Manager Automation?

choices.text: Run Command executes a single ad hoc command or script on one or more managed instances, while Automation orchestrates multi-step workflows that can span multiple AWS API actions and resources, not just instance-level commands
Run Command and Automation are the same feature under two different console menu names
Automation can only target on-premises servers, while Run Command only targets EC2 instances
Run Command requires a Lambda function to execute, while Automation does not

explanation: Run Command is designed for immediate, one-off execution of commands or scripts on managed nodes, while Automation executes structured, multi-step runbooks that can call various AWS service APIs beyond instance commands, such as creating snapshots or modifying security groups. Both features can target EC2 and hybrid on-premises managed instances, and neither requires Lambda for basic steps, although Automation can invoke Lambda as one step type.

stem: A CloudOps engineer must ensure that a specific antivirus agent configuration and a required set of registry settings remain applied on a fleet of managed EC2 instances on an ongoing basis, automatically correcting any instance that drifts from the desired state. Which Systems Manager capability is designed for this?

choices.text: Systems Manager State Manager
Systems Manager Session Manager
Systems Manager Automation with a one-time execution
Systems Manager Distributor

explanation: State Manager associates a document with managed instances and enforces a defined state on a recurring schedule, automatically reapplying configuration when drift is detected. Session Manager is for interactive access, a one-time Automation execution does not provide ongoing enforcement, and Distributor packages and deploys software rather than continuously enforcing configuration state.

stem: An Automation execution using the AWS-managed document AWS-RestartEC2Instance fails at a step with the error AccessDenied when attempting to call ec2:RebootInstances. The engineer manually has permission to reboot the instance in the console. What is the most likely explanation?

choices.text: The IAM role that the Automation execution assumes does not have the ec2:RebootInstances permission, even though the engineer's own IAM identity does
Systems Manager Automation always runs using root AWS account credentials and cannot be denied
The EC2 instance's operating system is blocking the API call at the network layer
AWS-RestartEC2Instance is deprecated and no longer functions in any Region

explanation: Automation executions run under an assumed IAM role, separate from the calling user's own permissions, so a missing permission on that role causes AccessDenied even if the user could perform the action interactively. Automation does not use root credentials, an OS-level restriction would not produce an IAM AccessDenied API error, and AWS-RestartEC2Instance remains a valid AWS-managed document.

stem: Which AWS service allows a CloudOps engineer to create rules that match patterns in events from AWS services, SaaS partners, or custom applications, and route matching events to targets such as AWS Lambda functions, Step Functions, or SNS topics?

choices.text: Amazon EventBridge
Amazon SQS
AWS Step Functions
Amazon Kinesis Data Streams

explanation: Amazon EventBridge is a serverless event bus service that ingests events, matches them against rules, and routes them to a wide range of targets, forming the backbone of event-driven automation. SQS is a message queue without rule-based routing across sources, Step Functions orchestrates workflows but is not itself an event bus, and Kinesis Data Streams handles real-time data streaming rather than event pattern matching and routing.

stem: A CloudOps engineer wants to automatically tag every newly launched EC2 instance with the name of the IAM principal that launched it, without requiring developers to change their launch process. Which event-driven approach accomplishes this?

choices.text: Create an EventBridge rule that matches EC2 RunInstances events recorded by CloudTrail and triggers a Lambda function that reads the event details and applies the appropriate tags
Configure an S3 bucket notification that fires whenever an EC2 instance starts
Schedule a Systems Manager Run Command to run every hour and tag any untagged instances found
Ask developers to manually add a required tag field in the EC2 launch wizard

explanation: EventBridge can match CloudTrail-recorded API events like RunInstances in near real time and invoke a Lambda function that inspects the event payload, including the identity of the caller, to apply tags immediately after launch. S3 notifications are unrelated to EC2 launch events, a scheduled Run Command introduces delay and only catches untagged instances after the fact, and relying on manual developer action does not guarantee automation.

stem: A CloudOps engineer needs an S3 upload to trigger a workflow that involves matching against multiple content-based filters and routing to several different targets, including a Step Functions state machine and an SNS topic, with the ability to archive and replay events later. Compared to configuring S3 bucket notifications directly, what is an advantage of enabling EventBridge notifications on the bucket instead?

choices.text: EventBridge supports advanced content filtering and can fan out matching events to multiple, varied targets in the same account or across accounts, and provides archive and replay of events, capabilities that direct S3 bucket notifications do not offer
Direct S3 bucket notifications support more target types than EventBridge, including Step Functions
EventBridge cannot be used with S3 at all, only with EC2 and CloudTrail events
Direct S3 bucket notifications automatically retain a 90 day replay log by default

explanation: Routing S3 events through EventBridge unlocks advanced event pattern matching, multiple simultaneous targets across accounts, and archive-and-replay capability, which native S3 bucket notifications do not provide. Native S3 event notifications support only Lambda, SNS, SQS, and EventBridge as targets, not Step Functions directly, and they do not include a built-in replay log.

stem: An EventBridge rule targets a Lambda function to remediate noncompliant security group changes, but CloudWatch metrics show the rule is matching events successfully while the Lambda function's invocation count remains at zero. What is the most likely cause?

choices.text: The Lambda function's resource-based policy does not grant the EventBridge service principal permission to invoke the function
The Lambda function's runtime has been deprecated by AWS
The EventBridge rule's event pattern is too broad and is matching too many events
The Lambda function's memory allocation is set too low to start execution

explanation: For EventBridge to invoke a Lambda function as a target, the function must have a resource-based policy statement granting the EventBridge service principal permission to invoke it; without it, the rule shows as matching but the invocation silently fails to reach the function. A deprecated runtime would cause invocation errors rather than zero invocations, an overly broad pattern would increase invocations rather than suppress them, and low memory allocation affects performance, not whether the function is invoked.

stem: Which AWS Systems Manager capability provides a central location where operational issues, called OpsItems, related to AWS resources are aggregated along with contextual data and related runbooks, to help engineers investigate and resolve issues faster?

choices.text: Systems Manager OpsCenter
Systems Manager Inventory
Systems Manager Patch Manager
Systems Manager Distributor

explanation: OpsCenter aggregates operational issues as OpsItems and surfaces related resource data, metrics, and runbooks in one place to speed up investigation and remediation. Inventory only collects metadata about installed software and configuration, Patch Manager automates patching, and Distributor packages and deploys software, none of which serve as a centralized operational issue dashboard.

stem: A scheduled EventBridge rule using a cron expression is intended to invoke a Systems Manager Automation runbook every day at 6:00 AM UTC to stop nonproduction EC2 instances, but the rule has never triggered the runbook. The rule shows as enabled and its event pattern section is empty since it is schedule based. What should the engineer check next?

choices.text: Whether the IAM role attached to the EventBridge rule has permission to call ssm:StartAutomationExecution
Whether the S3 bucket policy allows EventBridge to read objects
Whether the target EC2 instances have the Systems Manager Agent uninstalled
Whether the rule's cron expression uses local time instead of UTC, since EventBridge only accepts local time zones

explanation: A scheduled rule that targets an Automation runbook must use an IAM role with permission to call ssm:StartAutomationExecution; without that permission, the invocation fails silently rather than the rule not firing. S3 permissions are unrelated here, a missing SSM Agent would affect a runbook's instance-level steps but not prevent an Automation execution from starting, and EventBridge schedule expressions are defined in UTC, not local time, so that option's premise is also wrong.

stem: After a recurring incident where developers accidentally leave large, unattached Amazon EBS volumes provisioned, a CloudOps engineer wants to automatically identify and delete unattached volumes older than 7 days every night, with an approval step required before deletion in production accounts. Which approach best satisfies this requirement?

choices.text: Create a Systems Manager Automation runbook that identifies unattached volumes and includes an approval step, then trigger it on a schedule using an EventBridge scheduled rule
Configure an S3 lifecycle policy to delete EBS snapshots older than 7 days
Use AWS Budgets to send an alert when EBS costs increase
Manually review the EC2 console every night before leaving the office

explanation: Systems Manager Automation supports approval steps within a runbook, and pairing that runbook with a nightly EventBridge scheduled rule fully automates detection while preserving a manual gate before any destructive action in production. S3 lifecycle policies apply to S3 objects, not EBS volumes, AWS Budgets only alerts on cost thresholds without taking remediation action, and manual nightly review is not automation.

stem: A CloudOps team uses Amazon DevOps Guru to detect operational anomalies in their serverless application. They want any new DevOps Guru insight to automatically create a ticket in their incident management system and, for a specific known issue pattern, trigger a Systems Manager Automation runbook to remediate it without waiting for a human to check the DevOps Guru console. Which architecture enables this?

choices.text: Configure an Amazon EventBridge rule that matches DevOps Guru insight events and routes them to targets such as a Lambda function for ticket creation and a Systems Manager Automation runbook for remediation
Enable a DevOps Guru built-in auto-remediation feature that directly executes Systems Manager runbooks with no other services involved
Poll the DevOps Guru console API every minute using a cron job on an EC2 instance to check for new insights
Configure DevOps Guru to write insights directly into an RDS database and use RDS triggers to invoke Lambda

explanation: DevOps Guru publishes insight and anomaly events to Amazon EventBridge, so a rule can match those events and fan out to multiple targets, such as a Lambda function that creates a ticket and a Systems Manager Automation runbook that performs remediation, without manual console checks. DevOps Guru does not have a built-in direct-to-runbook auto-remediation feature bypassing EventBridge, polling the console API is unnecessary given native event integration, and DevOps Guru does not write insights into RDS.

stem: A CloudOps engineer must ensure that every IAM user in an AWS account sets a password with a minimum length of 14 characters, at least one uppercase letter, one lowercase letter, one number, and one symbol, and that passwords expire after 90 days. Which AWS feature should the engineer configure to meet this requirement?

choices.text: An IAM account password policy
A permissions boundary attached to each IAM user
A Service Control Policy applied to the account
An AWS Config managed rule with automatic remediation

explanation: The IAM account password policy is the account-level setting that enforces password length, complexity, and expiration requirements for IAM users. Permissions boundaries control the maximum permissions a user can have, not password complexity, and SCPs govern API actions rather than password rules, so neither can enforce this requirement directly.

stem: A security team wants to require that the root user and all IAM users with console access use a hardware or virtual MFA device before performing any sensitive action. Which statement about MFA in IAM is correct?

choices.text: MFA can only be enabled for the root user, not for individual IAM users
A single virtual MFA device such as an authenticator app can be assigned to multiple IAM users simultaneously
IAM supports virtual MFA apps, U2F security keys, and hardware TOTP devices, and each device can be assigned to only one IAM identity at a time
Enabling MFA automatically forces all existing IAM access keys to be rotated
MFA devices registered in IAM automatically satisfy Amazon Cognito authentication requirements

explanation: IAM supports multiple MFA device types, including virtual authenticator apps, FIDO security keys, and hardware TOTP tokens, and each device is bound to a single IAM user or the root user. MFA can be enabled for both the root user and individual IAM users, so A is wrong, and enabling MFA has no effect on access key rotation or Cognito, making D and E incorrect.

stem: A CloudOps engineer notices that a CloudTrail trail's log files stored in Amazon S3 may have been tampered with after delivery. Which CloudTrail feature should be enabled to detect whether a log file has been modified or deleted after it was delivered?

choices.text: CloudTrail Insights
Log file integrity validation
Server-side encryption with SSE-KMS on the trail
CloudTrail Lake

explanation: Log file integrity validation generates a hash for each delivered log file and periodic digest files that can be used to cryptographically verify that log files have not been altered or deleted after delivery. CloudTrail Insights detects unusual API activity patterns, and SSE-KMS protects confidentiality but does not by itself provide tamper detection.

stem: A CloudOps engineer wants to identify any S3 buckets or IAM roles in the account that are accessible from outside the AWS Organization, without manually reviewing every resource policy. Which service should be used?

choices.text: AWS IAM Access Analyzer
AWS Trusted Advisor performance checks
Amazon Macie
AWS Config aggregator

explanation: IAM Access Analyzer continuously analyzes resource policies, such as those on S3 buckets, IAM roles, and KMS keys, and generates findings that identify resources shared with external entities outside the specified zone of trust. Macie focuses on discovering sensitive data in S3, and Trusted Advisor performance checks are unrelated to external access findings.

stem: A developer reports that an application using an IAM role cannot call the ec2:DescribeInstances action, even though the attached policy appears to allow it. The CloudOps engineer wants to test the effective permissions of the role for this specific action before making any changes. Which tool should be used first?

choices.text: AWS Config rule evaluation history
The IAM Policy Simulator
AWS CloudTrail Lake query
Amazon Inspector network reachability analysis

explanation: The IAM Policy Simulator lets an administrator test and troubleshoot identity-based and resource-based policies by simulating whether a specific action would be allowed or denied, including the effect of any SCPs or permissions boundaries, without making a live API call. CloudTrail Lake shows historical events that already occurred, and Config and Inspector do not evaluate hypothetical IAM permission checks.

stem: A company is restructuring its multi-account AWS environment using AWS Organizations. It wants production workloads and development workloads to have different sets of guardrails, while still allowing centralized billing and consolidated CloudTrail logging across all accounts. What is the best way to organize the accounts?

choices.text: Place all accounts directly under the organization root and apply one SCP to the entire organization
Create separate organizational units for production and development, and attach different SCPs to each OU
Create a separate AWS Organization for production and another for development
Use IAM Identity Center permission sets instead of Organizational Units to separate production and development guardrails

explanation: Creating separate organizational units for production and development and attaching distinct SCPs to each OU allows different sets of guardrails while keeping all accounts under a single organization for consolidated billing and centralized logging. Using one SCP for the whole organization would not differentiate guardrails, and separate organizations would lose the benefits of consolidated billing and centralized management.

stem: What is the primary purpose of a permission set in AWS IAM Identity Center (successor to AWS Single Sign-On)?

choices.text: It defines a collection of IAM policies that are provisioned as an IAM role in one or more AWS accounts for assigned users or groups
It replaces the need for a password policy on federated users
It stores the encryption keys used to protect Secrets Manager secrets
It is a Service Control Policy that is automatically attached to every organizational unit
It is a CloudTrail configuration that logs sign-in events for federated users

explanation: A permission set in IAM Identity Center is a template of IAM policies that IAM Identity Center uses to provision an IAM role in the target AWS accounts, defining what assigned users or groups can do once they sign in. It is unrelated to password policies, KMS keys, SCPs, or CloudTrail logging configuration.

stem: A CloudOps engineer wants a quick, automated way to check whether the AWS account root user has MFA enabled, whether any security groups allow unrestricted access to specific high-risk ports, and whether IAM access keys are older than 90 days, without writing custom Config rules. Which AWS service provides these checks out of the box?

choices.text: AWS Trusted Advisor
Amazon Inspector
AWS Well-Architected Tool
AWS Audit Manager

explanation: Trusted Advisor includes prebuilt security checks such as root account MFA status, security groups with unrestricted ports, and IAM access key rotation, surfacing them as a dashboard without requiring custom rule authoring. Inspector focuses on vulnerability and network reachability findings for workloads, and the Well-Architected Tool and Audit Manager provide broader review frameworks rather than automated point-in-time account checks.

stem: A CloudOps team must demonstrate compliance with an internal security baseline across dozens of AWS accounts by grouping multiple related AWS Config rules together and deploying them consistently through AWS Organizations. Which AWS Config feature should be used?

choices.text: A single custom Config rule with multiple Lambda triggers
A conformance pack
An aggregator authorization
A Config recorder with multiple delivery channels

explanation: A conformance pack is a collection of AWS Config rules and remediation actions that can be packaged as a single entity and deployed across an organization to check compliance with a common framework or baseline. An aggregator only consolidates compliance data for viewing across accounts, and a Config recorder simply records resource configuration changes rather than grouping rules.

stem: A company operates in multiple AWS Regions and wants a single CloudTrail configuration that automatically captures management events from every current and future Region into one Amazon S3 bucket, rather than creating a separate trail per Region. What should the engineer configure?

choices.text: A separate trail in each Region, each delivering logs to its own regional S3 bucket
A single multi-Region trail that applies to all Regions, including any Regions enabled in the future
AWS Config aggregators configured in each Region
CloudTrail Insights enabled globally with no trail required

explanation: A multi-Region trail automatically applies to all Regions, including Regions that are enabled after the trail is created, and delivers events to a single specified S3 bucket, which is the recommended approach for comprehensive account-wide logging with minimal management overhead. Creating separate per-Region trails works but requires far more operational effort and does not automatically cover new Regions, and Config aggregators consolidate configuration compliance data rather than CloudTrail events.

stem: A company is designing a data classification scheme for objects stored in Amazon S3 so that operations staff can quickly identify which buckets contain regulated customer data versus public marketing assets. Which approach best supports this goal using native AWS features?

choices.text: Apply resource tags such as data-classification=confidential to buckets and objects, and use those tags to drive access policies and automation
Rename every bucket to include the word confidential or public in the bucket name
Rely solely on S3 Storage Class to distinguish sensitive data from public data
Store a spreadsheet of classifications outside AWS and manually cross-reference it during audits
Use S3 Transfer Acceleration status as an indicator of data sensitivity

explanation: Tagging buckets and objects with classification labels is the standard native mechanism for identifying data sensitivity, and those tags can be referenced in IAM policies, Config rules, and automation to enforce controls consistently. Bucket naming conventions and storage class or transfer settings are not designed to convey data sensitivity and do not integrate with policy-based enforcement the way tags do.

stem: A CloudOps engineer requests a public TLS certificate through AWS Certificate Manager (ACM) for a domain and chooses DNS validation. What must occur before ACM will issue the certificate?

choices.text: The engineer must upload the private key of an existing certificate authority to ACM
A CNAME record provided by ACM must be added to the domain's DNS configuration to prove control of the domain
The domain must be transferred to Amazon Route 53 permanently
The engineer must manually approve an email sent to the domain's WHOIS contact

explanation: With DNS validation, ACM provides a CNAME record that must be added to the domain's DNS zone, and ACM issues the certificate once it detects that record, which also enables automatic renewal as long as the record remains in place. Email validation, not DNS validation, involves approving a message sent to domain contacts, and the domain does not need to be transferred to Route 53, only have the required record added to its authoritative DNS.

stem: After enabling automatic rotation for a database secret in AWS Secrets Manager, an application begins receiving authentication failures immediately after each rotation cycle. What is the most likely cause the CloudOps engineer should investigate first?

choices.text: The rotation Lambda function does not have network connectivity or permissions to update the credential on both Secrets Manager and the target database
Secrets Manager does not support rotation for database credentials
The application is using an IAM role instead of a database username and password
KMS automatic key rotation is disabled for the default aws/secretsmanager key

explanation: A common cause of post-rotation authentication failures is that the rotation Lambda function cannot reach the database, for example due to VPC or security group misconfiguration, or lacks the permissions to update credentials on both the secret and the database, leaving them out of sync. Secrets Manager fully supports rotation for common database engines, and KMS key rotation of the encryption key used to protect the secret does not affect the secret's credential values.

stem: An Amazon GuardDuty finding indicates UnauthorizedAccess:EC2/SSHBruteForce for an EC2 instance. What does this finding type indicate, and what is an appropriate first response action?

choices.text: It indicates repeated failed SSH login attempts against the instance from a potentially malicious source, and the engineer should review and tighten the security group rules and investigate the source IP
It indicates that the instance's root volume is unencrypted, and the engineer should enable EBS encryption
It indicates that the instance is missing an AWS Config conformance pack, and the engineer should deploy one
It indicates that the instance's IAM role has excessive permissions, and the engineer should attach a permissions boundary
It indicates that CloudTrail logging has stopped for the account, and the engineer should re-enable the trail

explanation: The UnauthorizedAccess:EC2/SSHBruteForce finding means GuardDuty observed a pattern consistent with an SSH brute-force attack targeting the instance, so restricting inbound SSH access through security groups and investigating the source is an appropriate immediate response. The other options describe unrelated issues, such as unencrypted volumes, missing conformance packs, excessive IAM permissions, or disabled logging, none of which this specific finding type reports.

stem: A CloudOps engineer wants a single dashboard that aggregates and normalizes security findings from GuardDuty, Inspector, and AWS Config, presenting them with a consistent severity scoring format, and that also supports checking resources against standards such as the AWS Foundational Security Best Practices. Which service should be used?

choices.text: AWS Security Hub
Amazon Macie
AWS Trusted Advisor
Amazon CloudWatch Logs Insights

explanation: Security Hub aggregates, normalizes, and prioritizes findings from multiple AWS security services such as GuardDuty, Inspector, and Config using the AWS Security Finding Format, and it also runs automated checks against security standards like the AWS Foundational Security Best Practices. Macie is focused specifically on discovering sensitive data in S3, and Trusted Advisor and CloudWatch Logs Insights do not provide this cross-service finding aggregation and standards-based scoring.

stem: A CloudOps engineer wants to automatically discover known software vulnerabilities and unintended network exposure on Amazon EC2 instances and container images, without deploying a third-party scanning agent. Which AWS service is designed for this purpose?

choices.text: Amazon Inspector
AWS Config
Amazon Macie
AWS Firewall Manager

explanation: Amazon Inspector automatically and continuously scans EC2 instances and container images stored in Amazon ECR for software vulnerabilities and unintended network reachability, without requiring manual agent deployment on supported workloads. Config evaluates resource configuration compliance rather than vulnerability scanning, Macie focuses on sensitive data discovery in S3, and Firewall Manager centrally manages firewall rules rather than scanning for vulnerabilities.

stem: After adding a new NACL rule to explicitly deny inbound traffic from a malicious IP range on a subnet, legitimate clients outside the VPC suddenly cannot complete TCP connections to instances in that subnet, even though the deny rule has a higher (later evaluated) rule number than existing allow rules. What is the most likely cause?

choices.text: NACL rules are evaluated in random order, so the deny rule is sometimes applied first
The security group attached to the instances is now blocking the traffic instead
The new deny rule number is lower than an existing outbound ephemeral port allow rule, so it is evaluated first and blocks return traffic for unrelated connections
NACLs cannot contain both allow and deny rules in the same rule set

explanation: NACL rules are evaluated in ascending numeric order and the first match wins, so a lower-numbered deny rule takes effect before higher-numbered allow rules, even if it was intended to target only the malicious range. If the rule's number or CIDR scope is too broad or ordered incorrectly, it can inadvertently block or interfere with legitimate stateless return traffic. NACLs evaluate rules in a defined numeric order (not randomly), can mix allow and deny, and this scenario is not about security groups since NACL rule ordering is the described change.

stem: What is the primary purpose of Amazon Route 53 Resolver DNS Firewall?

choices.text: To provide authoritative DNS hosting for public domain names
To filter and control outbound DNS queries from resources in a VPC, blocking or allowing queries based on domain lists
To load balance DNS queries across multiple Availability Zones
To encrypt DNS traffic between on-premises resolvers and Route 53

explanation: Route 53 Resolver DNS Firewall lets you create domain-list-based rules to allow, block, or monitor outbound DNS queries made by resources inside a VPC, helping prevent DNS exfiltration and access to known malicious domains. It is not for authoritative public DNS hosting (that is Route 53 hosted zones), does not perform DNS load balancing, and does not itself provide DNS-over-TLS/HTTPS encryption between resolvers.

stem: A company wants deep packet inspection and intrusion prevention capabilities (such as signature-based threat detection) applied to traffic flowing between its VPC and the internet, beyond what security groups and NACLs provide. Which AWS service should be deployed?

choices.text: AWS WAF
AWS Network Firewall
Amazon GuardDuty
AWS Shield Standard

explanation: AWS Network Firewall is a managed stateful, network-layer firewall that supports intrusion prevention signatures, deep packet inspection, and domain/IP filtering for VPC traffic. AWS WAF (A) operates at Layer 7 and protects web applications (HTTP/HTTPS) behind CloudFront, ALB, or API Gateway, not general VPC network traffic. GuardDuty (C) is a threat detection service, not an inline firewall, and Shield Standard (D) provides baseline DDoS protection without deep packet inspection.

stem: A company wants to distribute DNS query traffic across two EC2-based application endpoints in proportions of 70% and 30% for A/B testing purposes. Which Amazon Route 53 routing policy should be used?

choices.text: Latency-based routing
Weighted routing
Failover routing
Geolocation routing

explanation: Weighted routing lets you assign relative weights to multiple records for the same name, controlling the proportion of DNS responses (and thus traffic) sent to each endpoint, which is ideal for A/B testing or gradual rollout. Latency-based routing (A) selects the endpoint with the lowest latency for the requester rather than a fixed proportion, failover routing (C) is for active-passive DR, and geolocation routing (D) routes based on the requester's geographic location.

stem: A global SaaS company has application stacks deployed in the us-east-1, eu-west-1, and ap-southeast-1 regions. It wants each user's DNS query to be answered with the record for whichever regional endpoint currently provides the fastest round-trip response for that user, and to automatically shift if network conditions change. Which Route 53 routing policy best satisfies this requirement?

choices.text: Simple routing with a single record listing all three IP addresses
Geolocation routing based on the user's country
Latency-based routing across records in all three regions
Multivalue answer routing

explanation: Latency-based routing returns the record associated with the AWS Region that gives the lowest network latency for the requester, based on continuously measured latency data, which adapts to changing network conditions. Geolocation routing (B) routes strictly by the user's geographic location regardless of measured latency, simple routing (A) provides no intelligent selection, and multivalue answer routing (D) returns multiple healthy records without latency awareness.

stem: A media company must ensure that users located in a specific country are directed only to a compliance-approved regional endpoint that stores their data locally, per local regulation, regardless of which endpoint would be fastest for them. Which Route 53 routing policy should be configured?

choices.text: Latency-based routing
Geolocation routing
Weighted routing
Multivalue answer routing

explanation: Geolocation routing routes DNS queries based on the geographic location of the requester, which allows a company to enforce data residency or regulatory requirements by directing users in a specific country to a designated endpoint. Latency-based routing (A) would instead pick the fastest endpoint even if it violates compliance requirements, and weighted (C) or multivalue (D) routing do not consider requester location at all.

stem: What information does Amazon Route 53 Resolver query logging capture?

choices.text: HTTP request and response headers for web traffic passing through a VPC
DNS queries made by resources within a VPC (or through a Resolver endpoint) and basic information about the responses
Network packet payloads for all traffic traversing an ENI
IAM API calls made against Route 53 hosted zones
TCP connection metadata for load balancer traffic

explanation: Route 53 Resolver query logging records DNS queries originating from resources in a VPC, along with details such as the domain queried, query type, and response, which can be delivered to Amazon S3, CloudWatch Logs, or Kinesis Data Firehose. It does not capture HTTP headers or packet payloads (that would be VPC Flow Logs or a packet capture tool), and IAM API call auditing is handled by AWS CloudTrail, not Resolver query logs.

stem: A company has an on-premises data center connected to its AWS VPC via AWS Direct Connect. It needs resources in the VPC to resolve DNS names hosted on on-premises DNS servers, and it also needs on-premises servers to resolve names in a Route 53 private hosted zone associated with the VPC. What should be configured?

choices.text: A single Route 53 Resolver outbound endpoint only, with no additional configuration needed for on-premises to VPC resolution
Route 53 Resolver outbound endpoint with forwarding rules for on-premises domains, and a Route 53 Resolver inbound endpoint to allow on-premises resolvers to query the VPC's private hosted zone
A public Route 53 hosted zone shared with the on-premises network over the internet
AWS Direct Connect automatically handles DNS resolution in both directions with no Resolver endpoints required

explanation: Bidirectional hybrid DNS resolution requires both endpoint types: an outbound endpoint with conditional forwarding rules lets VPC resources send specified domain queries to on-premises DNS servers, while an inbound endpoint provides IP addresses that on-premises servers can query to resolve records in the VPC's private hosted zone. An outbound endpoint alone (A) only covers VPC-to-on-premises resolution, a public hosted zone (C) is unnecessary and insecure for private records, and Direct Connect (D) provides network connectivity only, not DNS resolution logic.

stem: A company serves its website through Amazon CloudFront with a single origin, an Application Load Balancer in one AWS Region. To improve availability if the primary origin becomes unhealthy, the company wants CloudFront to automatically serve requests from a secondary origin in another Region without requiring a DNS change. What should be configured?

choices.text: A Route 53 health check with failover routing pointing directly at the ALB, bypassing CloudFront
A CloudFront origin group with the primary and secondary origins, configured with origin failover based on specified HTTP status codes
Two separate CloudFront distributions with a weighted Route 53 record between them
A single CloudFront origin with a custom error page that redirects to the secondary Region

explanation: CloudFront supports origin groups, where you define a primary and a secondary origin plus a set of failover status codes; if the primary origin returns one of those codes or fails to respond, CloudFront automatically retries the secondary origin. This happens within CloudFront itself with no DNS change needed. Option A removes CloudFront from the path entirely, option C is more complex and depends on DNS propagation, and a custom error page (D) cannot dynamically redirect to fetch different origin content the way origin failover does.

stem: A company wants to point its apex (zone root) domain, example.com, directly at a CloudFront distribution, but standard DNS rules prohibit a CNAME record at the zone apex. What Route 53 feature should be used instead?

choices.text: A Route 53 alias record pointing to the CloudFront distribution
A TXT record containing the CloudFront domain name
A PTR record for reverse DNS lookup
A standard CNAME record, since Route 53 has no restriction on apex CNAMEs

explanation: Route 53 alias records let you map an apex domain to AWS resources like CloudFront distributions, ELB load balancers, or S3 website endpoints, functioning like a CNAME at the zone apex without violating DNS standards, and without incurring a query charge when the target is an AWS resource. TXT (B) and PTR (C) records serve entirely different purposes, and standard CNAME records are still not permitted at the zone apex per DNS RFC rules, even in Route 53.

stem: An engineer configured a Route 53 Resolver outbound endpoint and a forwarding rule to send queries for corp.example.internal to an on-premises DNS server over a Direct Connect connection. EC2 instances in the VPC still fail to resolve names in that domain. Security groups on the outbound endpoint allow outbound DNS (port 53) to the on-premises DNS server IP, and the rule is confirmed present. What should the engineer check next?

choices.text: Whether the forwarding rule has been associated with the VPC where the EC2 instances reside
Whether the EC2 instances have an assigned public IP address
Whether Amazon CloudFront is configured for the domain
Whether a Route 53 public hosted zone exists for corp.example.internal

explanation: A Resolver forwarding rule only takes effect for VPCs it is explicitly associated with; if the rule was created but never associated with the target VPC, queries from that VPC will not be forwarded per the rule. Public IP addresses on EC2 instances (B) are unrelated to DNS forwarding, CloudFront (C) has no role in DNS resolution logic, and a public hosted zone (D) is unnecessary and inappropriate for an internal, on-premises-resolved domain.

stem: An EC2 instance launched in a public subnet with an assigned public IPv4 address cannot reach the internet, while other instances in the same subnet work fine. The instance's security group allows all outbound traffic. What should the engineer check first?

choices.text: Whether the instance's operating system firewall or route table entries within the instance itself are misconfigured, and whether the subnet route table has a route to an internet gateway
Whether a VPC peering connection exists
Whether the instance is using a gateway VPC endpoint
Whether AWS Shield Advanced is enabled

explanation: Since other instances in the same subnet work, the subnet-level route table and NACL are likely fine, so the issue is more likely instance-specific: an OS-level firewall, incorrect local network configuration, or an accidentally modified route/NACL association on that ENI. Confirming the subnet has a 0.0.0.0/0 route to an internet gateway is still a reasonable baseline check. VPC peering (B) and gateway endpoints (C) are unrelated to general internet access, and Shield Advanced (D) is a DDoS protection service, not related to outbound connectivity failures.

stem: Instances in a private subnet can successfully send outbound requests to an external API, but the responses never arrive back at the instances, even though the security group allows all outbound traffic and the security group's default stateful behavior should permit the return traffic. What is the most likely cause?

choices.text: The route table associated with the subnet is missing a route to a NAT gateway
The subnet's network ACL allows the outbound request but does not have an inbound rule permitting the ephemeral port range used for the return traffic
The security group is missing an outbound rule
The instances are not using an Elastic IP address

explanation: Because the request successfully leaves the subnet, the route table and outbound path are working, ruling out A. NACLs are stateless, so even if the security group (stateful) allows the traffic, the NACL must separately have an inbound rule allowing the ephemeral port range (typically 1024-65535) for return traffic to reach the instance. The security group already allows all outbound traffic per the scenario, ruling out C, and private subnet instances communicating via NAT do not require their own Elastic IP (D).

stem: An engineer is investigating why certain traffic to an EC2 instance is being dropped. They enable VPC Flow Logs on the relevant ENI and see log entries with the action field set to REJECT for the traffic in question. What does this indicate?

choices.text: The traffic was throttled due to instance CPU credit exhaustion
The traffic was denied by a security group or network ACL rule associated with the ENI or subnet
The traffic was successfully delivered but the application returned an HTTP 4xx error
The traffic was routed to the wrong Availability Zone

explanation: In VPC Flow Logs, the REJECT action specifically indicates that a security group or NACL denied the traffic at the network layer before it reached the application, which is exactly the kind of connectivity issue Flow Logs are designed to surface. Flow Logs operate below the application layer, so they do not reflect CPU credits (A) or HTTP status codes (C), and Flow Logs do not report cross-AZ routing errors (D) as a REJECT action.

stem: Two VPCs, VPC-A and VPC-B, are both attached to the same AWS Transit Gateway. Instances in VPC-A can ping instances in a third VPC, VPC-C, also attached to the Transit Gateway, but VPC-A instances cannot reach VPC-B instances at all, despite security groups and NACLs allowing the traffic in both VPCs. What is the most likely root cause?

choices.text: VPC-A and VPC-B have overlapping CIDR blocks, which is not permitted through a Transit Gateway
The Transit Gateway route table associated with VPC-A's attachment does not have a route to VPC-B's CIDR, or VPC-B's attachment was not properly propagated/associated in that route table
Transit Gateway only supports connectivity between two VPCs at a time
VPC-B must be peered directly with VPC-A even when both use Transit Gateway

explanation: Since VPC-A can already reach VPC-C over the same Transit Gateway, the TGW attachments and basic connectivity work, so the most likely cause is a missing route to VPC-B's CIDR in the Transit Gateway route table associated with VPC-A (via missing route propagation or association), which is a common Transit Gateway routing table misconfiguration. Overlapping CIDRs (A) would typically cause consistent failures and are not implied here, Transit Gateway supports many VPC attachments simultaneously (contradicting C), and direct peering (D) is unnecessary when both VPCs already use Transit Gateway.

stem: A security team wants to identify which specific AWS WAF rule is blocking a set of legitimate customer requests to a web application behind CloudFront. Which log source should they examine?

choices.text: VPC Flow Logs
AWS WAF logs (or the WAF sampled requests view), which record the rule that matched and the action taken for each web request
Amazon Route 53 Resolver query logs
AWS CloudTrail management event logs

explanation: AWS WAF logs (delivered via Kinesis Data Firehose, S3, or CloudWatch Logs) and the WAF console's sampled requests both show which rule within a web ACL matched a given request and whether it was allowed, blocked, or counted, making them the correct source for this investigation. VPC Flow Logs (A) capture network-layer traffic metadata, not HTTP-layer WAF rule matches; Resolver query logs (C) capture DNS queries; and CloudTrail (D) records API management events, not individual web request inspections.

stem: A company has a Site-to-Site VPN connection between its VPC and an on-premises data center using a virtual private gateway and dynamic (BGP) routing. On-premises servers can reach some VPC subnets but not others that were added to the VPC after the VPN was originally established. Static routing is not in use. What is the most likely cause?

choices.text: The new subnets' CIDR ranges are not being advertised over BGP from the customer gateway side, or route propagation from the virtual private gateway into the relevant VPC route tables was not enabled for the new subnets
Site-to-Site VPN connections support a maximum of two subnets per VPC
BGP routing cannot be used with AWS Site-to-Site VPN and must be switched to static routing
The virtual private gateway must be recreated whenever a new subnet is added to the VPC

explanation: With BGP-based dynamic routing over Site-to-Site VPN, connectivity to a given CIDR depends on that range being advertised by the on-premises side and, on the AWS side, on route propagation being enabled from the virtual private gateway into the route tables of the new subnets; missing either results in exactly this partial-reachability symptom. AWS Site-to-Site VPN has no such two-subnet limit (B), fully supports BGP dynamic routing (contradicting C), and does not require gateway recreation when subnets are added (D).

stem: Users report intermittent 502 Bad Gateway errors when accessing an application through Amazon CloudFront, which uses an Application Load Balancer as its origin. The engineer wants to determine whether the errors originate from CloudFront, the ALB, or the backend targets. Which combination of logs provides the most complete picture?

choices.text: Only VPC Flow Logs, since they capture all HTTP status codes returned by any resource
CloudFront access logs to see the response codes CloudFront returned to clients, combined with ALB access logs to see target response times and status codes returned by the backend targets
Only AWS WAF logs, since 502 errors are always caused by WAF rule evaluations
Amazon Route 53 query logs, since DNS resolution issues are the primary cause of 502 errors

explanation: CloudFront access logs show what CloudFront returned to the end user and from which origin, while ALB access logs record target_status_code and target_processing_time, revealing whether the ALB or its registered targets are the source of failures; together they let you trace the error along the full request path. VPC Flow Logs (A) only capture IP-layer connection metadata, not HTTP status codes; 502 errors are not caused by WAF rule evaluation (C), since WAF returning a block would show as 403, not 502; and DNS resolution (D) would cause connection failures, not a 502 response from an established connection.
